intro: LS1 has no Pro pages on the site: this is a C2 extension of the same topics (routines, useful expressions, phrasal verbs, healthy habits), for revision and for the exam.
order: Learning Path 1 (a warm-up) and Learning Path 6 (the final product) have no new vocabulary or grammar.
gintro: One C2 grammar point per Learning Path, with practice in the style of C2 Proficiency key word transformations (3–8 words, including the word in CAPITALS) and open cloze.

vocab.name: Routine and time
items: a creature of habit
someone who always does the same things in the same way
My dad is a creature of habit: same breakfast every day.
like clockwork
happening regularly and exactly as planned
The 7.42 bus arrives like clockwork.
the daily grind
the boring, tiring routine of work or school
By Thursday the daily grind starts to wear me down.
to be stuck in a rut
to be in a boring situation that never changes
I felt stuck in a rut, so I joined the climbing club.
at the crack of dawn
very early in the morning
Bakers start work at the crack of dawn.
to burn the midnight oil
to work or study late into the night
I burnt the midnight oil before the exam.
to cram (something) in
to fit a lot of activities into a short time
We crammed in three museums in one afternoon.
to fritter away (time)
to waste time on unimportant things
I frittered away the evening on my phone.
to while away (the hours)
to spend time pleasantly when there is nothing else to do
We whiled away the afternoon playing cards.

vocab.name: Collocations
items: a gruelling schedule
an extremely tiring timetable
Athletes keep a gruelling training schedule.
to keep regular hours
to go to bed and get up at the same times
Keeping regular hours helps you sleep better.
to snatch (a bite / some sleep)
to get a little of something quickly, when you can
I snatched a sandwich between classes.
a hectic pace
a very busy, fast rhythm
I can't keep up this hectic pace much longer.
to be pressed for time
to have very little time
Sorry, I'm a bit pressed for time today.

grammar.title: Habits at C2: always, will / would, tend to, used to
how: Present continuous + always / constantly / forever for a habit that annoys you: He's always borrowing my charger.

will / would for typical, characteristic behaviour (present / past): She'll sit there for hours. · As a child I would spend every summer at the beach. Stressed WILL shows irritation: He WILL leave his socks on the floor.
tend to / be prone to / be inclined to for general tendencies: Teenagers tend to go to bed late. · I'm prone to oversleeping on Mondays.
used to + infinitive (past habit, now finished) vs be / get used to + -ing (be / become accustomed): I used to walk to school. · I'm used to getting up early. · I'm getting used to the new timetable.
Exam tip: would is not possible for past states: I used to have (not would have) long hair.
practice: My brother leaves his things everywhere, which drives me mad. ALWAYS → My brother ___ his things everywhere.
Present continuous + always for an annoying habit.
When I was little, my grandmother read to me every night. WOULD → When I was little, my grandmother ___ every night.
would for a repeated past action.
Teenagers generally go to bed later than adults. TEND → Teenagers ___ bed later than adults.
Getting up at six is no longer hard for me. USED → I ___ up at six.
am used to getting / have got used to getting
I had a long journey to school in primary, but not any more. USED → I ___ a long journey to school in primary.
Past state: used to, not would.
I often oversleep on Mondays. PRONE → I ___ on Mondays.
Open cloze: She ___ sit by the window for hours, just watching the street. (characteristic behaviour)
Open cloze: It took me months to get used ___ the new timetable.

vocab.name: Phrasal verbs: the day
items: to drag yourself out of bed
to get up with great difficulty
On Mondays I have to drag myself out of bed.
to lie in
to stay in bed later than usual
On Sundays I lie in until ten.
to turn in
to go to bed
I'm shattered: I'm going to turn in.
to nod off / to doze off
to fall asleep without meaning to
I nodded off during the film.
to wind down
to relax gradually after activity or stress
Reading helps me wind down before bed.
to squeeze in
to manage to fit something into a busy timetable
Can you squeeze in a quick coffee?
to get round to
to finally do something you have been meaning to do
I never got round to answering her message.
to knuckle down
to start working hard and seriously
With exams next week, it's time to knuckle down.

vocab.name: Idioms
items: to call it a day
to stop working for the day
We've done enough: let's call it a day.
to bite the bullet
to do something unpleasant that you have been avoiding
I bit the bullet and started my project.
to hit the ground running
to start something with energy and speed
After the holidays I want to hit the ground running.
to be on the go
to be very busy and active all the time
I've been on the go since seven this morning.
a night owl / an early bird
someone who is most active late at night / early in the morning
I'm a night owl: I can't think before ten.

grammar.title: Discourse at C2: concession and contrast
how: Much as / Although / While + clause: Much as I love weekends, I find them hard to organise.
albeit + adjective / adverb / phrase (= although): a useful, albeit tiring, routine.
Despite / In spite of / Notwithstanding + noun or -ing: Despite going to bed early, I felt exhausted. (never despite of)
Adjective / adverb + as / though + subject + verb: Tired as I was, I finished my homework.
Linking two sentences: That said, … · Even so, … · Be that as it may, … · Nevertheless, …
practice: Although I love weekends, I find them hard to organise. MUCH → ___ weekends, I find them hard to organise.
I was very tired, but I finished my homework. AS → Tired ___ , I finished my homework.
I went to bed early, but I still felt exhausted. DESPITE → ___ to bed early, I still felt exhausted.
It's a useful routine, although it's tiring. ALBEIT → It's a useful, ___ , routine.
Open cloze: In spite ___ the noise, I slept well.
Open cloze: The plan is ambitious. That ___ , it's worth trying.
Open cloze: Hard ___ she tried, she couldn't wake up before nine.
Open cloze: Be that as it ___ , we still have to finish by Friday.
Fixed phrase: be that as it may.

vocab.name: Phrasal verbs with nuance
items: to fall behind (with)
to fail to keep up with work or a schedule
I fell behind with my reading when I was ill.
to keep up with
to move or learn at the same speed as others
It's hard to keep up with all my subjects.
to cut down on
to reduce the amount of something
I'm trying to cut down on screen time.
to cut out
to stop eating or doing something completely
She cut out fizzy drinks.
to come down with
to start to suffer from an illness
I came down with flu the day before the trip.
to burn out
to become exhausted from working too hard
If you never rest, you'll burn out.
to bounce back
to recover quickly after a problem
She bounced back after a bad first term.
to put up with
to accept something annoying without complaining
I can't put up with the noise any longer.
to face up to
to accept and deal with a difficult situation
You need to face up to the problem.

grammar.title: Present tenses at C2: stative verbs and the present perfect continuous
how: Stative verbs with two meanings: I think it's late (opinion) vs I'm thinking of joining a gym (considering). Also have, see, taste, appear, be: He's being difficult (behaving, temporarily).
Present perfect continuous for an activity with visible results or for emphasis on duration: I've been revising all afternoon, so I'm shattered.
Present simple for scheduled events and in time clauses about the future: The train leaves at 7.15. · I'll call you when I get home.
Phrasal verbs: with a pronoun object, separable verbs must be split: turn it off (not turn off it); three-part verbs never split: put up with it.
practice: I am considering joining the climbing club. THINKING → I ___ the climbing club.
am thinking of joining / am thinking about joining
He is behaving very rudely today. BEING → He ___ today.
I started revising at two and I'm still doing it. BEEN → I ___ two o'clock.
I can't tolerate this noise any longer. PUT → I can't ___ this noise any longer.
Open cloze: Switch the TV off, please. → Switch ___ off, please. (pronoun)
Open cloze: I'll text you as soon as I ___ home. (arrive)
Present simple in future time clauses.
I'm trying to eat less sugar. CUT → I'm trying to ___ sugar.
She recovered quickly after a bad start. BOUNCED → She ___ after a bad start.

vocab.name: Health and well-being
items: sedentary
involving a lot of sitting and little exercise
A sedentary lifestyle is bad for your heart.
sleep deprivation
not getting enough sleep over a period of time
Sleep deprivation affects concentration.
to be glued to (a screen)
to look at something constantly
He's glued to his phone all evening.
in moderation
in reasonable, not excessive, amounts
Sweets are fine in moderation.
wholesome
good for your health or your well-being
a wholesome breakfast
to take its toll (on)
to have a gradual harmful effect
Late nights took their toll on my grades.
to stave off
to stop something bad from happening for a time
A short walk staves off the afternoon slump.
well-being
the state of being healthy and happy
Exercise improves mental well-being.
to recharge your batteries
to rest so that you have energy again
A weekend in the mountains recharges my batteries.

grammar.title: Advice and hypothesis at C2
how: It's (high / about) time + past simple: It's high time you went to bed.
would rather + past simple (someone else): I'd rather you didn't eat in my room.
Inverted conditionals (formal): Were you to sleep more, you'd feel better. · Had I known, I'd have gone to bed earlier. · Should you feel unwell, rest.
Formal advice: You'd be well advised to… · It might be worth + -ing… · If I were in your shoes, I'd…
But for / Without + noun = if it were not for: But for my alarm, I'd never get up.
practice: You should go to bed now; it's late. TIME → It's ___ to bed.
high time you went / about time you went
If you slept more, you'd feel better. WERE → ___ more, you'd feel better.
If I had known about the test, I would have revised. HAD → ___ about the test, I would have revised.
I'd prefer you not to use your phone at dinner. RATHER → I'd ___ your phone at dinner.
rather you did not use / rather you didn't use
If it weren't for my alarm, I'd never get up. BUT → ___ alarm, I'd never get up.
It would be a good idea for you to cut down on caffeine. ADVISED → You'd ___ down on caffeine.
Open cloze: It might be worth ___ (try) a new routine.
Open cloze: If I ___ in your shoes, I'd talk to the coach.
